title: Data analyst

manager.name: Wei
manager.title: Director of Merchandising
manager.persona_note: Wei lost a great person and wants that again. A good recruiter finds what made them great, not who they were.

teaser: Wei leads the buying team at an online store and wants a copy of the analyst who just left.
context: The company sells home goods online and has about 120 people.
The analyst works with Wei's buying team, who decide what to stock.
message: Hi, our analyst Alex just left, and it's a big loss for the buying team. I'd love to find someone just as good.
The job ad is Alex's old one, so it's a starting point.
Do you have ten minutes to go over what we need?
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Wei will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to explain the numbers clearly to the buying team, so they stock the right products.
needs.n2: Someone to build the data systems behind the website.
needs.n3: Someone to run tests on the website.

beats.label: Another Alex
beats.sam: Our analyst Alex just left, and honestly, I'd love another Alex. Alex was perfect.

choices.text: That's a big loss. What did Alex do that made the biggest difference to your team?
choices.reply: Every Monday, Alex told us which products to reorder, in plain words we could act on.
choices.why: Asking what made someone great turns 'find me another Alex' into skills you can actually look for.

choices.text: Would it help if I looked for people with a background as close to Alex's as possible?
choices.why: Copying someone's background is tempting, but it may not be what made Alex good at the job.

choices.text: You know it's unlikely we'll find an exact copy of Alex, right?
choices.why: Pointing out the obvious makes the manager defensive and doesn't move the search forward.

choices.text: Was there any part of the job Alex was less keen on, or that you'd like done differently?
choices.reply: Big technical projects. Alex just wanted to help us make decisions.
choices.why: A follow-up on the gaps helps you avoid hiring for strengths the job doesn't need.

choices.text: So Alex was strong at pretty much everything?
choices.why: A leading question gets a vague yes. An open one would have found the detail you need.

choices.text: Before we go on, do you know why Alex decided to leave the company in the end?
choices.why: It's natural to wonder, but it felt personal and you lost a little goodwill.

beats.label: The degree
beats.sam: They must have a statistics degree. Alex did.

choices.text: Did Alex use advanced statistics day to day, or was it more about explaining the numbers?
choices.reply: Explaining, really. And come to think of it, Alex studied history.
choices.why: Checking a must-have against the person you're replacing often shows it was never what mattered.

choices.text: That's helpful to know. Should I make the statistics degree a firm requirement for everyone I put forward?
choices.why: Agreeing narrows the search on a guess about what made Alex successful.

choices.text: So the degree is really what made Alex so good, in your view?
choices.why: A leading question gave the wrong reason a yes, and now it shapes the search.

beats.label: Working together
beats.sam: They'll mostly work on their own, the way Alex did.

choices.text: Who will they work with most closely, and how do those people like to get information?
choices.reply: The buyers. They want a short, plain summary every Monday, not a big report.
choices.why: Asking who the analyst serves tells you which skills matter most, which here is clear, simple communication.

choices.text: Do you prefer someone who works independently, then?
choices.why: It's a fair question, but it builds a filter around a working style instead of the job.

choices.text: Should I look for someone who prefers to keep to themselves, like Alex?
choices.why: Screening on personality rather than skills shuts out good people and misses what the buyers actually need.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: Same pay as Alex had, I'd say.

choices.text: Is Alex's range still current, or has it moved since they joined?
choices.reply: $80,000 to $92,000. HR updated it this year.
choices.why: Old pay can be out of date. Checking keeps the search realistic and fair.

choices.text: Should I use Alex's salary as the target, then?
choices.why: You don't actually know what Alex earned, so you still can't tell who's affordable.

choices.text: Do you think Alex might have been underpaid, and that's why they left?
choices.why: Guessing about a former employee's pay sounds like criticism of the company, and it costs you goodwill for no benefit.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Office days
beats.sam: They'll be in the office two days a week, with the buyers.

choices.text: Two days alongside the buyers makes sense. What happens on those days, so I can describe it to candidates?
choices.reply: The Monday buying meeting, mostly. The analyst's numbers drive the whole discussion.
choices.why: Accepting a reasonable request, then asking what happens on those days, shows curiosity and gives you a real selling point for candidates.

choices.text: Could it be one day a week for the right person?
choices.reply: Two works better for the team.
choices.why: It's a fair question, but asked before you understand why those days matter, it can sound like you're already negotiating against the manager.

choices.text: Most analysts I talk to want to be fully remote. Could we drop the office days?
choices.reply: This one needs to be with the buyers.
choices.why: Pushing to change a settled decision, with nothing to back it up, spends goodwill you'll need for the questions that actually change the search.

choices.text: What decisions do those dashboards help the buyers make?
choices.reply: What to reorder, and what to stop selling.
choices.why: Asking what a task is for shows you the real job, and the real job is what you'll screen for.

choices.text: Should I focus on people with strong dashboard skills and experience with the tools you use?
choices.why: Agreeing describes a tool, not the job the tool is meant to do.

choices.text: Aren't dashboards the easy part of an analyst's job?
choices.why: Downplaying the manager's words starts a debate instead of a conversation, and you learn nothing about the decisions behind the work.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Honestly, it's a pretty standard analyst job.

choices.text: What would make a great analyst want this job over the others they'll see?
choices.reply: Their advice goes straight into what we sell, and they see the results within weeks.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive gives you the pitch for the right person.

choices.text: Should I keep the job description simple and standard, then?
choices.why: You'd miss what makes this job different, and that's what attracts strong people.

choices.text: Do you think a strong analyst would see it as standard?
choices.why: Questioning the manager rarely changes their view. Asking what makes the job appealing gives you something you can actually use.

candidates.name: Avery
facts: Wrote a weekly reorder report for buyers
Buyers changed orders based on it

reason.n1: Wrote a weekly report that changed what buyers ordered, in plain words. That's what made Alex great, and it fits the range.

view.n1: Avery does what Alex did, maybe better.

candidates.name: Linden
candidates.job: Senior analyst at a grocery chain
facts: Interested in building the company's data systems

reason.n1: Works on the right decisions, but is keen to build data systems. Wei said Alex skipped the big technical projects to help the team decide.

view.n1: Linden would build us something impressive. We need answers on Monday.

candidates.name: Parker
candidates.job: Data scientist at a research lab

reason.n1: The degree matches the old ad, but Wei confirmed the job is about explaining the numbers simply, and Alex didn't need the degree.

view.n1: Parker is Alex on paper, not in practice.
